item.title: 123. Locutions
item.dc:creator: Antonio de Arcas
item.description: When one doesn't seem to get it, He speaks loud and clear. In my last letter I wrote about how the thoughts "I think what you need is silence" and "Don't…
item.content:encoded:
In my last letter I wrote about how the thoughts "I think what you need is silence" and "Don't plan" guided my entire life into a desert. The letter was dense, and I did not want to overload it. But I left out something so beautiful that today I am dedicating this letter to it.

When I stepped back from my mentors and in general from all the voices that claimed to know what was best for me, more space opened up in my life. Without thinking too much about it, I devoted that space to studying the life, figure and message of Jesus, and my days began to unfold more and more in his company. There came a point when I began to experience, once again, what Saint John of the Cross called locutions: interior conversations with Him.

One day, quietly sweeping the dry leaves from the terrace and feeling very lonely, I asked:

— Lord, where do I belong?

I meant which spiritual or religious group was most suited to me. His answer was simply:

— In me.

That answer was not merely a thought. It had a profound effect on my soul. It was as if, in my solitude, anxious branches had grown in my soul reaching outward for contact. When I received that answer, I felt all those branches being cut, and my soul being drawn back to its center, where Christ shone as my true home and my true company.

Another time, walking through a park at the end of the day, I felt Him take my hand and join my walk. That gesture alone filled the air with a love that made me cry. Whatever worry or loneliness had been in my mind dissolved in the substance of his Presence. I said:

— Thank you for being here with me.
— I am always here. Thank you for being here with me!

And so began a conversation in which he answered my questions one by one. Like the experience I described above, his answers were not only words. They were more like infinite thoughts where one part, the crest of the wave, was verbal, but underneath there was an oceanic response, an ineffable energetic movement that illuminated some aspect of reality. By directing my attention in that way, the truth, always consoling, produced a corrective effect on my soul.

Sometimes his answers were brief:

— Lord, did you suffer?
— For everyone.

Others were more elaborate:

— Am I doing well not planning and living day by day?
— Yes, you are on the right track. {In a non-verbal way, he reminds me that, at this point, planning would come from a limited part of the mind, and that cannot be the will of God, which is total.}
— But sometimes one has to plan things.
— Yes, but those plans will come from wholeness and surrender, not from fear trying to control. Trust, rest in the will of the Father. It is much simpler than you want to make it. Your difficulty lies in accepting reality: because it is so hard for you to accept things as they are, you try to manipulate what happens so that things occur according to your preferences. If you learn to accept, that desire for control gradually becomes irrelevant.

And others were entirely non-verbal:

— Lord, sometimes I feel very alone.
{He directs my attention to a tree, and shows me something like "You are one with all life. There is only one life." In entering into communion with the tree, and through it with all life, solitude revealed itself, once again, as something simply impossible.}

Today he reminded me of an idea I had almost forgotten during these months of doubt and uncertainty: the one who asks questions is the ego, and I am not the ego.

So, as I gradually accept the reality that Jesus is always with me (and with everyone), the flowers of my initial fascination, laden with questions, are drying out, and in their place other fruits are growing: above all, the trust that I need not worry about anything. My life is His, He is my Shepherd, and it is not my role to tell him where we are going or how. His Presence is enough.

Instead of questions, He now simply sits beside me, and that instantly dissolves any suffering.

And if I am walking and feeling alone or afraid, He takes my hand. My half-closed hand, held in a hand of light, teaches me not to forget that He is always here with me.

And so we walk home, together and in silence.

With all my love,

Antonio

item.title: 122. Don't Plan
item.dc:creator: Antonio de Arcas
item.description: The hardest thing is to do nothing. Lately I have been praying the Our Father often, contemplating each phrase as the complete prayer it is. Thy will be…
item.content:encoded:
Lately I have been praying the Our Father often, contemplating each phrase as the complete prayer it is.

Thy will be done on earth as it is in Heaven.

What happens when one surrenders one's personal will?

"Your task is not to seek for love, but merely to seek and find all of the barriers within yourself that you have built against it."
- A Course in Miracles

The last time I was in Istanbul, Betül told me "I think what you need is silence."

After that, I began to feel an aversion to Instagram and abandoned my work there. I also stepped back from the mentors I had been working with, and mainly from their group sessions.

The idea "Don't plan" also returned, this time with a clarity and weight that left no room for negotiation. What I mean by that is that one day, after finishing breakfast, I stood up to put the dishes on the sink when, out of nowhere, a kind of syllogism crossed my mind:

I am what I am.

What is, is the will of God.

Therefore, what I am is the will of God.

This did not arrive simply as a thought. It was more like being struck by lightning, like putting my fingers in a socket and, in doing so, having a momentary vision of the entire electrical system of the world. Except that instead of the electrical system, I felt I was in communion with Creation, that is, with the will of God.

From that perspective, it was absolutely evident that I do not have an individual, separate, autonomous will. The individual will, by definition, would be the will of something that is not God’s will, and therefore the will of an illusion.

That experience shook me deeply. "Don't plan" was no longer just an invitation. It was an inevitability.

So I fell into a deeper level of self-abandonment, and my mind filled with fears and judgments. Those fears and judgments had always been there. I had been feeling them for years, pulling the strings from the shadows. Now, this surrender to inactivity provoked a resurgence of all that negativity, trying to force me back into action. What had once been a mafia operating in the shadows was now filling the streets with shootouts in broad daylight.

At the core, the fear was of being incapable of doing anything worthwhile with my life. All these gifts and talents going to waste under the command of a weak and scattered will. I put this under the microscope in my recent letter "120. Change of Owner."

During this difficult period I kept guiding the morning meditations and observed that there, and only there, that level of abandonment made sense. The more I let go of any desire for control and rested in the emptiness of the present moment, the more beautiful and healing the meditation I guided became.

The days passed, and my conscious mind did not know what to do or when to do it. Many days I did nothing, or at least nothing visible or practical. Some days I was incapable of the simplest tasks: replying to a message or making myself a meal. I was living firsthand the meaning of Jesus's words: "Without me you can do nothing."

Yesterday morning I went through another wave of fear and guilt. You have to pass through it. The gate of heaven is covered in thorns. I repeated once again the machete-prayer: "Holy Spirit, help me to see this with Love."

In the afternoon, Betül came home, as joyful and radiant as ever, and said "Okay, let's organize the afternoon: first we'll go return this package, then we can go to a café to work, then etc etc." I listened to her, happy on one side, a little tense on the other. "Ah! She's planning!" But I noticed such joy, simplicity and love in her words that it was evident this was good, and after two months of not planning anything at all, I surrendered to her plan and made it mine too.

The afternoon unfolded around it. I say around because sometimes we followed it perfectly, and other times we drifted. But it did not matter because everything was good, everything was held in love.

We ended up painting with watercolors some flowers that had been given to Betül for the engagement, and at the end of the day, on my way to brush my teeth, a lightbulb went on in my mind and I understood:

The entire process I just lived through with "don't plan" had as its purpose to take aim at my ego: all the dark and unreal identities that used to run my days. When I planned, I did it from demand, from the fear that wants to control, from desire that is never satisfied. I was in the hands of a blind tyrant, and this period has been a general strike to remove him from the throne.

Today, however, I could feel how Betül planned from intelligence, love and joy. It was clear that if we followed the plan it would have been a balanced and pleasant afternoon, and if we did not, it would have been perfect too.

This, once again, seems like the most obvious thing in the world when explained, but understanding something intellectually is one thing, and being it is another entirely. To be love, you have to let go of everything that is not love. You have to align with the truth, even if reluctantly, as in my experience of the syllogism, and let the creatures of the night stir before returning to the nothingness from which they came. The path is not easy, nor does it pretend to be. Salvation and the cross are inseparable.

Yesterday I discovered that, after two months clearing shadows, there was finally space in my mind to live a little closer to what Augustine captured in his beautiful commandment:

Love, and do what you will.

With all my love,

Antonio

item.title: 121. The Ideal Husband
item.dc:creator: Antonio de Arcas
item.description: Neurotic, scattered, full of shadows. Going after the princess of Istanbul!
item.content:encoded:
Going after the princess of Istanbul!

Tomorrow, God willing, Betül's parents will give me their daughter's hand in marriage. Wedding plans are complex, because we live in two different countries and come from two different traditions: Islam and Christianity. Everything is up in the air. Fortunately, the air too is in God's hands and we trust Him to show us when, where and how. For now, one step at a time, and while everything works itself out, we are preparing ourselves inwardly.

A few days ago, at night, sitting alone in front of a bonfire, I began to pray and asked God to make me the perfect husband for her. What I had in mind were all my flaws, my neuroses, my weaknesses and shortcomings, and I asked him to make me the most virtuous and luminous person in the world. But the light entered my mind and illuminated the truth:

"You already are what you are asking for. You are the ideal husband for her, exactly as you are now. The shadows you perceive in yourself are necessary for her process of salvation, just as hers are for yours. How else could she discover true love? Once again I remind you that you are perfect as you are now. Everything is perfect."

Stop and contemplate that, because it speaks of you too. Behind the veils of our mind, the judgments, beliefs, desires and aversions that distort our vision, you stand: a creation of God, as self-evident as you are mysterious. Wanting to be better than one is may sound loving, but it is at its core an attack that comes only from a misunderstanding of what we are. The perennial wisdom says "Know thyself," not "improve thyself."

What is truly and radically loving is to stop fighting what we are. God has a plan, and he did not make a mistake when he wrote your part.

With all my love,

Antonio

item.title: 120. Change of Owner
item.dc:creator: Antonio de Arcas
item.description: The previous one knew not what he did. What does it mean in practice to be "in the world but not of the world"?
item.content:encoded:
What does it mean in practice to be "in the world but not of the world"?

Is it really possible to change? To leave the past behind and adopt a new way of being in the world, more aligned with truth, love, and integrity?

These days have been an exercise in exactly that. I see my entire past: the many misaligned actions that led me to develop a poor self-concept, built on guilt and unworthiness. And that past arrives in my present moment like heavy waves trying to drown the new shoots.

A new identity is cultivated not by saying positive affirmations, but by taking actions that bear witness to that change. Every action is like a vote: Who am I? The timid, irresponsible Antonio, prone to laziness and dissociation, or the upright, courageous Antonio, aligned with his deepest understanding of the truth?

When the bag of past votes weighs so much, it is hard to believe it is possible to accumulate enough new votes to tip the balance toward the side I want.

This morning I was contemplating this and it seemed like an impossible battle to win, so I asked for help, and this is what the Holy Spirit showed me:

The past does not exist. It only occurs in the present, in the activity of our imagination, now. There is no scale where on one side sits the near-infinite weight of the past, and on the other the minuscule present trying to win with its infinitesimal weight. Only the present moment exists; there is nothing else. And in every moment we are contemplating a situation that invites us to choose: Who am I now?

The answer to that question is not irrevocably conditioned by the previous instant: this moment is not an effect of the previous one. Each instant is being created anew, and in this instant we are completely free to make a new decision. It makes no difference how many years we have lived from negativity. Only this present situation exists, and it is asking you: Who am I now?

When we accept the ego’s answer, our mind responds based on that supposed past, and our identity then seems to drag chains.

And yet we can also let the Holy Spirit answer for us, and his answer is: I am Spirit, I am free.

From there I see that the body is an instrument. Nothing more. It is not me, and nothing it does or has done defines or changes what I essentially am.

The body is like a guitar. If I walk onto a stage in front of thousands of people and, on the first chord, I realize the guitar is out of tune, how do I respond? The answer, again, will be a response to my question: Who am I now?

If, in a moment of madness, I believe that I am the guitar, I will feel shame, guilt for not having tuned it beforehand, and that moment will become a trauma that haunts me for the rest of my life saying: "you are not good enough."

If, on the other hand, I do not identify with the guitar and simply see it for what it is, an instrument, my response will probably be to stop for a moment, laugh, apologize, tune it, and try again.

In the same way, what my body did or did not do in the past does not define what I am. It makes no difference if I gave a thousand concerts with the guitar out of tune. That says nothing about the quality of the guitar itself, or about me as a musician. It only says that I did not yet have ears to hear, and that is not something to feel guilty about, but a natural process of maturation.

Returning to my present dilemma: I observe this moment, which is all that exists. I observe the ego's voice deploying its blind response: stories of guilt, shame, helplessness, anger. I observe everything from the distance the Spirit offers and ask: Who am I really? Am I this? Am I the out-of-tune guitar?

But I am not that. I am Spirit, I am a holy child of God, eternally innocent. What defines the center of my identity is the love of God, and from there I choose to forgive: I was mistaken in the past about who I was, and that led me to act erratically in the world. But now I am free to recognize the truth and act from there.

I take my body out of the ego's hands and give it to God. Change of owner. Here you go, God, I let You resolve this situation.

The body relaxes, the forehead softens, the mind empties.

Whatever happens next is not my concern, I surrender that to You as well.

Once again I have remembered and fulfilled my only function: to stop lending my ears to the ego and the noise of its illusory chains, and to listen to the Voice of God, which never ceases to say: "Not only have you been forgiven, but the effects of your errors have been completely cancelled. You are free."

With all my love,

Antonio

item.title: 119. Rage
item.dc:creator: Antonio de Arcas
item.description: Rage against the dying of the light. Terence McKenna used to say that "culture is not your friend." The concepts through which the world operates are too…
item.content:encoded:
Terence McKenna used to say that "culture is not your friend." The concepts through which the world operates are too small to guide what you truly are, and they only bring the confusion of someone who listens to too many voices.

An agitated surface hides the pearl at the bottom.

If you let yourself be guided by inherited and limited conceptions, you will receive an inherited and limited life. Meanwhile, your authentic life waits, glowing luminous beneath the opacity of ordinary existence.

What to do with the inner unease that stirs when one senses this?

There is a Sanskrit term, "samvega," which names a kind of inner roar that ignites when one realizes they have been living in a superficial way, out of alignment with the truth they sense at a deeper level. In that moment, the option of continuing as before becomes unbearable. The only way forward is not to change anything external, but to say "enough," to cross the inner wall of fear that rises when you abandon a prefabricated future, and to leap into the unknown guided only by love of the truth.

That is the spiritual zeal that gave the Zealots their name, except they directed that inner roar outward into violence. That is what the world does; that is what the spiritual ego does: feeling attacked, invaded, and subjected to a lie, it attacks the external forms that lie takes. That is Don Quixote charging at windmills.

Jesus felt a zeal like this when he entered the temple and found it full of thieves, but he did not turn toward violence. Against whom could he be violent, if not himself? Violence has no place in Christ, who is One. The only possible response is a deeper surrender: to let love lead you toward the death of what you’ve been, so that a wider and truer life can open. In his zeal to see God's will done on earth, Jesus chose the cross.

Do not go gentle into that good night. Rage, rage against the dying of the light. That is how Dylan Thomas expressed this same zeal, speaking not only of the death of the body, but of all the ways we settle for noise instead of the clarity silence, judgment instead of forgiveness, the slavery of the senses instead of the freedom of the soul.

We fall slowly, without wanting to notice it, into a conformism that is death in life. A comfortable and routine way of being that we sense is not the truth. Truth makes all things new, and that way of being is covered in dust. A mediocre novel written over the face of the living God. For a time we choose to stay there out of fear of discomfort, fear of what others will say, fear of the unknown, fear of what Love says we are.

But not today.

The light has awakened to itself, nearly extinguished beneath the grey crust of the world.

Rage, rage against the dying of the light.

With all my love,

Antonio

PS: That longing for a life more aligned with who you truly are does not necessarily require external changes, but an inner reordering, the acceptance of something within you that you have not yet embraced. In fact, the most beautiful and true thing in us is rarely really welcomed: "the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him." (Jn 1:10-11)

item.title: 118. A Cosmic Diamond
item.dc:creator: Antonio de Arcas
item.description: The ego has a value system, and you don't fit in it. From time to time, a deep truth breaks into the soul and produces a cataclysm in the ego. Last week I…
item.content:encoded:
From time to time, a deep truth breaks into the soul and produces a cataclysm in the ego. Last week I lived one of those moments. Here it is.

What is your value as a human being?

As always, there are two ways of seeing it: through the ego, or through the Holy Spirit.

The ego is the thought system built on separation. Once you accept the idea that you are an individual, autonomous being, an entire system grows from that seed, one that interprets what the world is, who others are, and who you are.

The Holy Spirit, on the other hand, is the part of your mind that has never forgotten that you are one with God and with the totality. From that knowing, a completely different system emerges, one that runs counter to the ego in every way.

So when we ask ourselves "What is my value?", the two answers could not be more different.

The ego assigns value based on what favors survival: your wealth, your education, your skills, your health, your capacity to produce or procreate. None of that has anything to do with the truth of who you are. It only speaks to how you interact with the world. Human value, seen this way, becomes highly variable and volatile. Where do the elderly fit in this system? The poor? The sick? At the bottom. The wealthy and influential will always come first, and the rest of us gradually feel ourselves diminished by comparison, until we reach the existential void of feeling useless and disposable.

The inequality we perceive in the world is unresolvable as long as we interpret reality through the ego. It does not matter how wealth is redistributed: some people will always be seen as more valuable than others.

The other day I began reading Magnifica Humanitas, the encyclical of Pope Leo XIV. A few minutes in, I had an experience that brought me great clarity and above all relief about my own value, and therefore about the value of every being. The encyclical places great emphasis on the intrinsic dignity and worth of the human person. But that day I felt small, incapable, useless, and I felt a sharp contrast between what I knew intellectually and what I was actually feeling. So I put the book down, sat with those feelings of smallness and unworthiness, turned my inner gaze upward, and with something like spiritual rage I prayed: "Holy Spirit, I know that my value is already infinite and cannot change, and yet here I am, feeling useless and worthless. If what you say is true, I want to know it now!"

The first thing I was shown was a symbol: a cosmic diamond. Try to hold that in your mind: a diamond the size of the universe.

Immediately after, I remembered perhaps the greatest gift I ever received through Joe, my teacher: we are the original thought of God. The first creative act of God was to create his Son and, through him, the world.

In that moment of need and supplication, the Holy Spirit brought me back to that “place,” and I recognized that my value lives there: I am a creator, not as an artist, but as a participant in the nature of the Son of God, made in his image and likeness. What the Holy Spirit showed me was the Christ in me, the eternal creative principle, the origin of life itself and therefore the essential identity of every living thing. There we are all truly equal, and our value is infinite because it is an extension of the value of God himself.

Seeing that, the feelings of smallness and incapacity were blown away, and one thought passed through my mind: "I want that one on my team!"

With all my love,

Antonio

item.title: 117. Surrendering to Commitment
item.dc:creator: Antonio de Arcas
item.description: Why we avoid it, and what we actually find when we accept it. Why are we afraid to follow our calling? Why do we resist choosing what we know is good for…
item.content:encoded:
Why are we afraid to follow our calling?

Why do we resist choosing what we know is good for us and for others?

Total commitment is not a matter of effort, but of surrender. To commit fully is to surrender completely to something, to let something be. That is why, when you commit totally, it becomes instantly easy: it is no longer you who carries it out, but God himself.

The fear of commitment, therefore, is really the fear of God; the fear of his will being done in your life.

The world speaks of fear of commitment, but what is truly frightening is not commitment, but its absence. Because the one who resists commitment is the ego, the illusion of having an individual will capable of deciding on its own. That is inseparable from fear, because it is the belief of being alone, facing an antagonistic world. A mind like that is fragmented and turned against itself. A mind like that is its own enemy. Without commitment, we live in doubt, in distraction, trying this and that, following a mind that does not know what it wants or where it is going.

Because the mind does not know. The best it can do is "know about," and that is not knowing. There is no certainty or true knowledge in it. Certainty belongs to the heart. And one can only truly commit to what one knows is true, and that is only known in the heart. Committing to something that is not true is like committing to a cloud. Commitment is either with the truth and is total, or it is not commitment.

When we commit to the truth, what we are really doing is surrendering to it. And when that happens, everything within us that opposes the truth will be triggered. That is the paradox of commitment: commitment to love leads us to experience our judgments and resentments. Commitment to peace shows us our conflicts. Commitment to certainty triggers doubts and confusion. Commitment to God and to others confronts us with our greatest enemy: the illusion we have made of ourselves. In short, commitment to the truth confronts us with everything that opposes the truth.

And what opposes the truth?

Fear: the fear of not being enough, of not being worthy of being loved, of the world discovering that we are in reality something dark, something guilty, something shameful, something unforgivable.

When you commit to the truth, all of that comes to the surface. The fear of commitment, therefore, is really the fear of facing our own deepest fears. But not facing them does not make them disappear; they simply stay in the shadow, blindly guiding our lives, keeping our minds wrapped in darkness.

That is why I walk hand in hand with Jesus, because he descended into those depths and passed through them, opening a path of light. To walk hand in hand with Jesus is to remember the Christ in you. It is to pass through hell knowing that you are invulnerable. You are still as God created you. No crucifixion can harm you. Salvation already is, and now at last you are claiming it.

And so the kingdom of fear ends and one opens to the Kingdom of God.

The commitment to that future which once terrified you is now revealed as surrender to the will of God.

The will of God is peace, joy, abundance and love.

The will of God is his Creation, his Being lovingly extended.

The will of God is you, the true you.

With all my love,

Antonio

item.title: 115. A Path of Gratitude
item.dc:creator: Antonio de Arcas
item.description: Always and everywhere. The good thing about not going to Mass very often is that when I do, I hear everything with fresh ears. Things I had been hearing…
item.content:encoded:
The good thing about not going to Mass very often is that when I do, I hear everything with fresh ears. Things I had been hearing my whole life in a semi-unconscious way suddenly surprise me. That was the case the other day, when I heard some words about gratitude.

At 21 I had already been contemplating the nature of reality for some time, and had developed some deep intuitions: that my mind was not contained inside my head, but was more like an antenna that could tune into different frequencies of thought; or that perception was in fact projection. But my first intuition of God, of the Father Creator, came to me one day while eating a steak.

I was in my last year of industrial engineering in Chicago. Alone in my apartment, watching the snow fall in slow motion on the other side of the window, with some pleasant music playing and eating a good steak. At that time I considered myself an atheist, but suddenly I felt a deep gratitude for the beauty of that moment, and it confronted me with the inevitable question: who am I grateful to? If I am appreciating this moment as though it were a gift, who gave it to me?

It is true that, if I was there at all, it was thanks to my father's financial support, so in part it was to him. But who could I thank for the beauty of that moment, the snow, the solitude, the music?

Without yet understanding it, my heart was opening and orienting itself again toward its origin, toward Home.

[10 YEARS LATER]

The other day I attended the wedding of a good friend. My joy and love for him, together with the beauty of the music and the church, made my heart open more than usual. The antenna of my mind tuned into the Spirit, and I began to listen with greater depth.

I then heard something I had heard hundreds of times before, but had never truly listened to until that moment:

It is truly right and just,

our duty and our salvation,

always and everywhere to give you thanks,

Lord, holy Father,

almighty and eternal God...

This is what I heard:

It is right.

It is right because God is the only source of all that is good. Being grateful to something created (like my earthly father) is already very good in itself, but in absolute terms it is stopping halfway: like thanking a reflection for the light of the Sun.

It is necessary.

God does not need our gratitude, but we do. Without it, we cannot appreciate what is good, and our perception gradually grows dark. Gratitude orients our mind toward God, who is the source of all good. Without it, we are denying that source, and therefore rejecting the good itself. Without gratitude we can accumulate treasures in this world, but not treasures of the heart.

It is our duty.

In this world we have many duties, all pulling at one another in an attempt to capture our attention. But in the true context of our existence, the Spirit, we have only one duty: to remember that we are one with God, our Self, and with all of Creation. A Course in Miracles calls this unique function "forgiveness." Dr. Hawkins called it "letting go." Here it is called "giving thanks." No matter the tradition, at heart it is all the same: releasing the grey interpretation the ego gives to this moment and choosing to contemplate it in the light of God. Everything is a gift. Do that always, and you will have fulfilled your destiny perfectly, regardless of the outward shape your life takes in this world.

It is our salvation.

Salvation from what? From the nightmare that results from believing we are separate from God. Gratitude reveals that, in reality, there is no separation at all. The union between what we give thanks for and God is more intimate than the union between light and the Sun. To be grateful to God is to be in Him.

Give thanks ALWAYS, and in ALL places.

Being grateful for pleasant things is good. But in my experience, gratitude has been most powerful when the situation has been hardest: when the pain seemed unbearable and hope was fading completely. In those moments, it is the ego that suffers and fights for its existence; but beyond it, your soul, your Spirit, crosses the threshold of a new birth. The most powerful thing you can do to pass through that ring of fire and completely dissolve resistance to transformation is to give thanks to God.

Then the happiness of the Spirit illuminates the mind and embraces the supposed misfortune. Pain and joy coexist like clouds and sky. Under that light, one sees that the situation is like the bitter but necessary medicine that an infinitely loving doctor brings to heal us.

A thank-you at the right moment has the power to transform catastrophe into blessing; it has the power to reveal that every instant is God wanting to offer us his gifts. A true thank-you opens the doors of our mind to His Presence, and lets the heart be filled with treasures.

A final note: what is worth giving thanks for?

Although it is good to be grateful for the things we have, we must observe whether our gratitude comes at the expense of others. Some examples might be feeling grateful for being healthy when someone falls ill, or for financial comfort when thinking of others living in poverty. That kind of gratitude, at the expense of what others lack, is in reality a form of attack. It is believing that God has favorites and treats some people more favorably than others. That is not the real God. The sun shines on everyone equally.

To be grateful to that partial god is to give thanks to something unreal, and therefore it is as though one were not grateful at all. The happiness derived from that form of gratitude comes from the ego, not the Spirit. It feels like temporary relief, but not like fullness.

If we want to experience true gratitude, the kind that opens the heart and unites our mind with its source, we must give thanks for the things we all receive equally.

We must give thanks that, although we tend to forget God, He never forgets us.

That his infinite embrace is always ready to heal our mind of its errors.

We must give thanks for the ways in which he guides us, out of darkness and toward the light, along the path most suited to each of us.

For how he gives us strength to face the difficulties of this world.

We must give thanks for the ways in which his light manifests in our lives, whatever form it takes.

We must give thanks even when we understand nothing, and especially then, when we understand nothing and are suffering. That thank-you will be like a prayer asking God: "show me what is real, for I have lost my way."

And we can also give thanks for the key itself: the word "thank you." One of the first words we ever learned, and probably the last we will say when everything is finally resolved at the end of time.

With all my love,

Antonio

item.title: 114. Watering with Unconditional Love
item.dc:creator: Antonio de Arcas
item.description: I'll admit judgment doesn't really work that well. As I let go of layer after layer of what I am not, I see more and more clearly that what I am is an…
item.content:encoded:
As I let go of layer after layer of what I am not, I see more and more clearly that what I am is an open field, a sky that nourishes with its light the garden where all beings appear. My work, then, is to be that light and, when clouds appear, not to forget that behind the clouds, the sun is still shining just the same.

All things are, at every moment, the best they can be. If they could be better, they would be. And all are good because they are a manifestation of life itself. Life can take forms with greater or lesser grace and harmony, but that judgment is arbitrary, relative, and irrelevant if what we seek is the Truth.

Truth, if it does not include unconditional love, cannot be the Truth.

Today, during a long and spontaneous meditation, this loving understanding turned toward me, and I saw myself under that benevolent light. Once again, I was shown that the only one who judges me is myself. Seeing myself this way, I understood why I deserve to be loved completely, and why there is no sense in blaming myself for the things I did or did not do.

I am exactly what I am at every moment, and I could not be any other way. Like a rose in the process of opening, perfectly fulfilling the role it must play at each point in its unfolding. There is no sense in blaming the rose for not having opened fully yet, nor does it make sense to demand it or force it to do so. Any attempt to force distorts and hinders the natural process, and will never reach the fullness that only love can inspire.

The best thing you can do with that rose you are is to love it, appreciate what it is in this moment, and give it the nourishment it needs to grow in the healthiest way possible.

God alone is responsible for the results. You are simply responsible for choosing the most favorable conditions. And that means choosing to sustain yourself in the energy of unconditional love, moment to moment, so that it is that energy that nourishes you and encourages you to open up to all that you are.

With all my love,

Antonio

item.title: 113. The Trunk
item.dc:creator: Antonio de Arcas
item.description: Too many branches to tend to? Find the trunk. In a world designed for specialists, generalists like me can easily fall into the trap of "jack of all…
item.content:encoded:
In a world designed for specialists, generalists like me can easily fall into the trap of "jack of all trades, master of none."

In this letter I share a great eureka moment that has unified, all at once, all the branches of my activity. From many things to do, to just one.

"Don't plan, let things happen for you."

With those words, my qigong teacher proposed a path for me to follow on my return to Madrid.

Five months later, my weeks are filled with activities that feel deeply aligned with my path. I didn't seek any of them. They simply came to me and I said "okay, I'm in." That's how friends, mentors, clients, partners and projects have arrived.

Despite the evident harmony of everything that's unfolding, these past few weeks I had the feeling that I was saying yes to too many things.

This week, however, I had a great eureka moment that showed me how, despite the apparent multiplicity of my activities, I am really only doing one thing.

When I saw this, I shared my discovery with Betül, who once again shone with one of her one-liners: "It's like a tree, and you've discovered the trunk."

She was right. If I felt like I was taking on too much, it was because I was putting my attention on the branches, trying to make them grow and bear fruit. From that angle, I felt all the branches competing for my attention. There never seems to be enough time or energy to nourish everything.

But all the branches converge in a trunk. And if I tend to the trunk, the branches receive what they need without me having to think about each one individually.

The trunk is the common denominator, the critical point of the system. The one place where, if I direct my attention, all other areas are affected.

The key to all of this lies in meaning. The branches represent not only different activities and areas of my life, but the purpose each one serves. When I look at the branches, each seems to have its own purpose: cooking to care for my body, creating content to reach more people, practicing music to cultivate my gift, doing qigong to keep my energy clean. It's impossible not to feel, from that perspective, that we are doing too many things. The purpose of my life seems to be divided into multiple facets, always competing with one another.

But there is a deeper purpose that sustains them all, the trunk that unifies and nourishes every branch: the trunk is, simply, to be happy. That is the central purpose that unifies all purposes.

What if, instead of doing each activity with its individual function in mind, I did it with that common purpose in mind?

What if instead of washing the dishes to keep the house clean, I did it to be happy while washing the dishes?

The difference is radical. Instead of forcing my mind to fulfill a thousand different functions, I focus it on just one.

Now, when I say be happy, I don't mean the temporary happiness that the things of this world offer. I mean the happiness that shines when I know myself, and I experience myself, as loved. It’s the joy of being aware that God's love is present, and that the entire universe sustains me in whatever I am doing.

Little by little my mind is opening to that reality that transcends my individual world, returning me to the awareness of that love which unites all things.

And how does one open to that loving presence?

By forgiving.

So we could take one step closer to the essence of the matter. The central purpose is not to be happy, but to forgive. Forgiveness opens the source of happiness. It cleans the window so that light can come through. Without forgiveness, resentments seem to deny the presence of love, and being happy is impossible without love.

The forgiveness I'm talking about is not moral forgiveness. It is letting go of everything that is not love.

Looking at that thought charged with negativity, recognizing its illusory nature and saying: "Holy Spirit, this is taking my peace away, and I want peace. I ask you to take this from me."

That is all I have to do, while washing the dishes, while driving, while making the bed, while using my phone, while writing or singing. That always takes me back to happiness, flow and ease.

From there, all things happen and arrange themselves on their own.

From there, it is no longer I who washes the dishes. When I align with love, my identity aligns with Love. I then experience what Paul expressed as "it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me." What I experience is that I have stepped aside, and Christ has stood up, and it is He who washes the dishes, for me, with all His Love.

With all my love,

Antonio

item.title: 112. I'm not sure I'm capable
item.dc:creator: Antonio de Arcas
item.description: Who are you choosing as your guide? I feel deeply grateful because I can see how all the pieces are falling into place. On the path toward God, all the…
item.content:encoded:
I feel deeply grateful because I can see how all the pieces are falling into place. On the path toward God, all the facets of life, once scattered and often at odds with one another, gradually unify under a single purpose.

All that is required to move in that direction is to follow the Holy Spirit, which is the part of your mind that has not forgotten that you are a child of God.

The other voice in your mind, loud and incoherent, is the ego, and it leads in the opposite direction: toward complexity, separation, and exhaustion.

Here is a letter addressed to the part of your mind that must make the key decision: Who do I listen to?

"I'm not sure I'm capable."

The other day I invited a member of Entre el Cielo y la Tierra (Between Heaven and Earth) to lead one of our group sessions herself, guiding a meditation she regularly practiced on her own. That was her response, tender and honest.

I want to share with you what I told her, because it came with the clarity of the Spirit not only for her, but also for me and for everyone.

I know there is something inside you that wants to come out into the world, something you want to do, a project waiting to be born. I share this message so that fear does not win that battle.

The key is in that "I'm not sure I'm capable." I know you are capable, if you weren't, we wouldn't even be having this conversation. The opportunity would not have arisen. You know it too, because one part of your mind (the Holy Spirit) has absolute faith in you, because it knows who you are and Who accompanies you at every moment.

The thing is, there is another part of your mind (the ego) that says something diametrically opposite: it tells you that you are weak, vulnerable, limited, and that it's better not to expose yourself to the world, lest the world discover and confirm that dark, small image.

When you say "I'm not sure I'm capable," what you are really saying is: "I don't know who I am: what the Holy Spirit tells me, or what the ego tells me."

Faith is holding on to the Spirit and acting from that place, despite the ego's complaints. And in acting, we discover that our faith was grounded in truth: who you are has no limit, you are perfect and loved exactly as you are, you are gifted with infinite power to do whatever you set your mind to, and everything always turns out far better than you had imagined.

That said, do what feels right to you. Often, when I feel pressured to do something, I ask myself: "What would love do?" There is no need to force anything. The goal is not to do things, it is to know who you are. You are love. Align with it, and if from that place doing scary things arises, wonderful. If not, it is wiser to say "no thank you" and embrace yourself knowing that all is well.

(I think I needed to remember this myself, so this message is as much for me as it is for you 🤍)

With all my love,

Antonio

item.title: 111. Life beyond the clouds
item.dc:creator: Antonio de Arcas
item.description: On cultivating inner freedom. There is nothing in this world that the Spirit cannot transform into a path of liberation, into a path toward God. I stepped…
item.content:encoded:
There is nothing in this world that the Spirit cannot transform into a path of liberation, into a path toward God.

I stepped onto the entrepreneurial path believing it would be about business, structure, strategy, sales, money and marketing.

Four months in, I'm beginning to realize it isn't. That's only the surface, and it must be studied and taken care of, of course. But at its core, this is the same as everything else. This, too, is about God, and my only function is to forgive.

This morning, in a conversation with the community, someone asked me: do you feel fear or anxiety about launching this new project? The answer is yes, but only in part. Thoughts of fear, insecurity, and doubt pass through my mind… but they are like clouds, and they say nothing about who I am. My work is to remain aware of the sky behind them, which is what I truly am: an open space of infinite potential. There, there is only total certainty. The certainty that this does not arise from me as a separate individual, but from an intelligence and a power far greater.

From there, my role is not to push this forward, but to allow it to be. The way to do that is to observe those thoughts with compassion and, seeing through them as the illusion they are, ask the Holy Spirit to dissolve them. That is all I have to do, and everything else unfolds on its own.

Throughout our lives, we have built an identity based on our history, on what we believe we are, on what others believe we are, on all the patterns of thought and emotion we have repeated again and again. All of that generates an energetic pattern, the ego, which is what we mistakenly call "I."

And what happens is that our consciousness, which is infinite, finds itself apparently trapped inside that character. Any sign of growth or change is interpreted as a threat, and so it tries to avoid all forms of novelty or adventure. We have built a cage for our soul, which, like everything that lives, wants to grow, expand, and fully enjoy the gift of life. Hence the phrase that always comes back to me from Dylan: "He not busy being born is busy dying."

Spiritual practice opens that inner space: it allows us to recognize our true vastness and the freedom that is our divine inheritance. As we cultivate that awareness, life begins to be lived differently, not from fear or scarcity, but from truth, where nothing is lacking. We stop building on sand and begin to build on rock.

This is why spiritual practice integrates so naturally with entrepreneurship and with any creative process. When beginning something new, that limited structure fires up and says: "I'm not capable, I'm not ready, who am I to do this?" But instead of stopping there, we ask for Help so that those apparent limitations may be dissolved, and we keep moving forward, with clarity, passing through the clouds, propelled by a strength and a joy that no thought or emotion can stop.

That capacity to transcend one's own mind is what is allowing me to move forward, to step out of who I thought I was, and begin embodying a wider identity in the world.

This is what I practice every morning before showing up to the daily meditation: I advance with my machete of light through the thicket of the limited self, which fights to maintain its smallness.

By the time I sit down in front of the screen at eight o'clock, I feel serene, expansive, fully surrendered. And then, from that stillness, I begin to guide a meditation where I teach the very capacity I have just practiced. Very meta!

With all my love,

Antonio

item.title: 110. Even blinking is too much work
item.dc:creator: Antonio de Arcas
item.description: There is an infinite strength that lifts us and guides us. This week marks one month since I opened a meditation group called Between Heaven and Earth. It…
item.content:encoded:
This week marks one month since I opened a meditation group called Between Heaven and Earth.

It has been a beautiful path.

Every morning, Monday through Friday, I have been guiding the same meditation, iterating, going a little deeper each day, letting go of the identities that would say, “who are you to teach this?”

The answer to that question has been arriving, again and again, at the climax of each meditation. And it does not speak only about me, but about all of us.

Today, I share it here as well.

Today I woke up tired. Thoughts about all the things I want to do began to pass through my mind, and almost immediately I felt overwhelmed, wanting to escape into my phone or go back to sleep. I felt that I did not have the strength to build the life I want. But that apparent weakness is not the problem; it is only a symptom of the oldest problem of all: the illusion of being separate, of believing that everything depends on ourselves and our limited strength.

There is another way.

An hour later, while guiding a meditation for my community, this idea returned to me:

For a sage, even blinking is too much work.

Years ago I heard this idea, and I did not understand it. Today I looked at it again, but this time under a much wider light, and this is what it showed me:

In reality, there is only one will, and it is the Will of God. There is only one intelligence guiding everything that happens, and that Intelligence has no divisions. Every time you blink, it is not you who does it, it is the entire Universe. There is no separation between your body and everything else. The whole Universe is required for you to take your next breath.

The human mind, before being trained, lives compressed within a body, believing itself to be isolated from everything else. From there, it thinks it is responsible for everything, and exhausts itself trying to control it all.

But within us lies the potential to blossom, to open the mind like a lotus flower with infinite petals. As this happens, our perspective expands radically. We begin to see that our mind is not separate from everything else. The deeper patterns that govern the world begin to reveal themselves. Our prayers begin to receive tangible answers. And mornings no longer feel the same, because we know that behind our apparent weakness, there is an infinite strength that lifts us and guides us.

In this way, we learn to lean more and more into that strength until, finally, even blinking is too much work.

With all my love,

Antonio

item.title: 109. We Can Only See in the Light
item.dc:creator: Antonio de Arcas
item.description: Are we the pot or the clay? Today I sat down before a blank page and, instead of bringing something already thought out to write about, I simply said…
item.content:encoded:
Today I sat down before a blank page and, instead of bringing something already thought out to write about, I simply said: "Lord, here I am. Guide me."

The result has made me very happy.

Thank you, Father, for this gift.

The Indian sage Ramana Maharshi attained Enlightenment spontaneously at the age of sixteen. One day, without being ill or anything of the sort, he suddenly felt, with absolute terror, that he was going to die. But instead of trying to flee or cry for help, he decided to investigate the experience of death. He lay down on the floor, went completely still as if already in rigor mortis, and asked himself: "This body dies. But what am I?"

He then recognized the "I Am" of God as his own identity, beyond all possibility of death. That awakening to eternal life came as a great flash of light.

We can only see in the light.

After that, he left his home, leaving behind a note that read: "I have set out from here in search of my Father and in obedience to His call." He boarded a train and made his way toward a sacred mountain called Arunachala, from which he would never again be parted.

After searching for a long time, his mother finally found him there, sitting, thin, and silent. In those days Ramana lived an ascetic life and did not speak. His mother urged him to come home with her, but he answered by writing this note:

"What is destined to happen will happen, no matter how hard you try to prevent it. What is not destined to happen will not happen, no matter how hard you try. Therefore, the best path is to remain in silence."

We can only see in the light.

But what is it that one sees in the light?

That you are not alone, and that what happens does not depend solely on you and your limited strength. You are immersed in the ocean that is the will of God. Your individual will is a small branch making its own leaves and fruit, but there is only one tree. There is only one Being. Ramana called it Atman; others call it Christ.

There is only one body: the Body of Christ, which includes the light that was created on the first day, the firmament on the second, the earth and its vegetation on the third, the sun, the moon and the stars on the fourth, the creatures of the sea and sky on the fifth, the land animals and the human being on the sixth.

The peace in the eyes of animals.

The total surrender of the trees that let all their leaves fall without lamenting, without even knowing that spring will come again afterward.

Everything shines with the same light, the same life and truth. There is nothing beyond that. Nothing can lie outside the infinite; nothing can be apart from its Source nor be of a different nature.

So what is our problem?

There is only one, and the young Ramana resolved it once and for all when he asked himself: "This body dies. But what am I?"

What one sees in the light is that the problem is already solved. Salvation is already complete; all is already forgiven. The body will die, but that is only a pot; the clay remains. The vessel says of itself: "Poor me, a sinner!"The clay is innocence.

The clay that forms us is no ordinary mud, it is the light of God. Clear the mind of ideas of separation, and all that remains is light without beginning, end, or division.

From there, you will see that your individual life follows the same loving will as all the rest of the Universe. You will see that everything is perfect as it is. Everything that happens is beneficial. The hand that shapes your days knows you and knows better than anyone what is best for you. Anxiety disappears and in its place shines trust. Fear disperses and wisdom remains. Anger gives way to compassion, and guilt to innocence. Joy envelops all things, and love reveals that all is one.

Today we celebrate the Resurrection, the glorious moment in which this truth redeemed the Universe. But that cosmic event is, at its heart, nothing more than the contrast between darkness and light. Only the light is real, and no one was ever born, nor will anyone ever die.

That is why, half a century later and already on his deathbed, one of his disciples said to Ramana:

"Bhagavan, you are leaving us."

To which He replied:

"Where could I go? I am here."

With all my love,

Antonio
